The problem

The reading app requests a large cover and a small text card together. Part of the cover response is lost, but the bytes for the text card arrive. Can the card still be shown?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Multiplexing lets multiple exchanges share a connection. Both HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 allow this, but the transport beneath them changes what happens during loss.

QUIC is a secure transport over UDP. UDP carries separate datagrams. QUIC adds its own recovery and provides independently ordered streams.

ProtocolWhere bytes have to be delivered in orderConsequence after the cover bytes are lost
HTTP/2 over TCPOne shared transport byte stream with a cumulative acknowledgmentLater text-card bytes can sit behind the gap if they occur after it in that stream.
HTTP/3 over QUICWithin each streamThe text card can advance if its own bytes and any compression or control information it depends on are available.

Even on QUIC, losing one packet can affect multiple streams if that packet contained their data. Congestion control also remains shared across the connection, so traffic may slow together even where delivery can progress independently.

The practical distinction is delivery waiting behind one missing range versus a shared reduction in sending rate. The first is an ordering dependency; the second is feedback about the network path.

Go deeperTrace the dependency before blaming the protocol
A lost QUIC packet carried data for both the cover and the card. Does their independent ordering ensure the card can finish immediately?

No. If the card needs bytes that were in that packet, its own stream has a gap. Stream independence helps when the other stream has what it needs.

Check yourself

The text bytes arrive after a missing cover range in the same TCP stream. Why can HTTP/2 wait?

Not quite. HTTP/2 can share a connection across both requests. Re-read that part ↑

Right. Separate HTTP streams share the TCP delivery order.

Not quite. The text bytes can be complete yet unavailable behind the TCP gap. Re-read that part ↑

In HTTP/3, the lost packet held only cover bytes. Card bytes and its dependencies are present. What is possible?

Not quite. Data is delivered by stream offset, not all packet numbers globally. Re-read that part ↑

Right. Each stream has its own ordering.

Not quite. Each stream still needs its own missing bytes. Re-read that part ↑

Both streams slow after network loss despite the card having no ordering gap. What could explain it?

Not quite. QUIC keeps the stream ordering independent. Re-read that part ↑

Right. Independent delivery can coexist with shared congestion feedback.

Not quite. Content identity is unrelated to shared congestion control. Re-read that part ↑

Sources
  • IETF RFC 9113: HTTP/2 streams and multiplexing
  • IETF RFC 9000: QUIC streams and loss
  • IETF RFC 9114: HTTP/3 connection and streams
  • IETF RFC 9002: congestion control

What you now know

HTTP/2 streams share one ordered TCP byte stream. HTTP/3 maps traffic onto independently ordered QUIC streams, so loss on one stream need not stop delivery on another.
